1	# Task 10: Domino chain reaction
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The scene is a tabletop with a curved line of 30 upright domino tiles (each a thin box, roughly 0.2 wide, 1.0 tall, 0.5 deep) spaced so that each tile can topple onto the next. A small heavy ball rests on a short ramp at the start of the line. A visible on-screen button labelled 'Release' lets the user roll the ball down the ramp, which strikes the first domino and starts a chain reaction in which the tiles topple one after another under real rigid-body physics (gravity, collisions, friction). A second button labelled 'Reset' restores every tile and the ball to the initial arrangement so the run can be repeated. Use a fixed physics timestep so the outcome is repeatable. Light the scene with a soft shadow-casting key light, give the table and tiles distinct materials, and frame the camera so the whole domino path is visible. Expose a read-only object window.__TASK_STATE__ = { phase: 'ready'|'running'|'settled', total: number, toppled: number, ballReleased: boolean } updated every frame, where a tile counts as toppled when it has tilted more than 60 degrees from vertical. Add no external network assets.

Quaternions are only available at build time, so at runtime I'll need to convert to Euler angles using the default ZYX order and three.js's standard formula, watching out for gimbal-lock singularities near 90° pitch.

I'll write my own ordered-Euler conversion rather than relying on a library export. For the domino's local thin axis mapped through yaw rotation, I derive toppling direction as yaw = atan2(-tz, tx), and compute tilt from vertical using the quaternion's up-vector component, flagging topple past 60°. For geometry, I'm settling on 0.2 thick by 1.0 tall dominoes spaced roughly 0.55-0.6 center-to-center so they can knock each other over.

With 30 dominoes at 0.5-0.55 spacing, the total path length runs 14.5-16.5 units, which is large for the viewport, so I'm considering a curved arc layout but need to check if a large sweep angle (over 100°) causes problems with the yaw-based Euler decomposition near singularities.

So instead I'll go with a gentler curve — something like a 90° total sweep with a larger radius (~9.2) — keeping the yaw angle within ±45° to stay well away from the Euler singularity while still giving a visually curved domino path.

So yaw angles up to ±70° stay safe from singularities, meaning I can use a generous sweep of around ±50° for the arc. I'm checking the geometry for a radius-8 arc spanning about 104°, computing chord length and sagitta to make sure it fits nicely within a 640x360 viewport.

This gives a bounding box roughly 12.6 by 3.1 units, nicely wide and short for the 16:9 frame. I'm now setting up the table dimensions and parameterizing the curved path the dominoes follow—placing them along an arc from -52° to +52° in angle, with the path curving in Z while moving along X, and planning a ramp to kick off the chain before the first domino.

Actually, reconsidering the arc so it starts heading along +X would push the yaw near 104° by the end, which risks gimbal lock in the Euler conversion near ±90°. The math stays technically exact there but gets ugly with large compensating x/z terms, so I should avoid that orientation and instead pre-rotate the whole path so the heading starts along +x more cleanly.

Simpler fix: sweep the curve only from -52° to 52°, placing the ramp toward the back-left with the table scaled to fit, and keep the camera looking from front-above so the arc bulges away from it rather than toward the extreme yaw case.

Now I'm working out table bounds and camera placement: x spans -10 to 10, z spans -3 to 9, with the camera positioned up and back at (0,14,14) targeting (0,0,2.5) with a 40° fov, checking that the visible width covers the arc properly.

For the ramp and ball, I need the ball to rest on a tilted static ramp without rolling off immediately once physics starts stepping -- since everything is dynamic from the start, I need a way to hold the ball in place until the release moment, maybe by constraining it initially or delaying the simulation step for that body.

I could instead always step physics but add a temporary stopper collider to hold the ball in place, though there's no obvious removeCollider hook on the controller side, so it's simpler to just not step until release. For reset, rather than relying on a world-level reset, it's safer to manually set each body's position, rotation, and zero out velocities/angular velocities and wake it — though I should keep in mind that Rapier's internal state might not be perfectly identical across runs even after a manual reset.

For true determinism, the cleanest approach is disposing the world entirely on reset and rebuilding a fresh world and bodies, reusing the same scene node handles so rendering stays stable. I need to check whether the engine's physics module can be synchronously recreated after the initial async preload, and confirm that body creation via descriptors properly applies material properties like friction and restitution.

I'm also thinking through timestep handling—using a fixed substep (like 1/120) and an accumulator pattern so the simulation steps deterministically regardless of frame rate, while variable step counts per frame don't break reproducibility as long as the sequence of fixed steps stays consistent.

For headless Chromium running at low frame rates, I need a clamp on max frame time (maybe up to 0.25s, allowing ~30 fixed substeps) so the simulation doesn't fall too far behind real-time when rendering is slow.

With ~35 bodies this is cheap computationally, but a full chain of 30 dominoes spaced at 0.55 units, each toppling in 0.15-0.25s, would take 6-8 seconds to complete in real-time -- a test waiting on this could need 20-30 seconds total.
